newsitem.title: USA: Staples predicts merger approval but talks continue.
newsitem.headline: Staples predicts merger approval but talks continue.

text.p: With discussions reaching a critical stage, a top official of Staples predicted Thursday that the government will approve the company's merger with Office Depot "in some fashion." But the outcome of the talks is uncertain.
The Federal Trade Commission has set an unusual Saturday meeting at which the deal is expected to be considered.
One option is that the commissioners could vote to ask a federal court to block the deal, a possibility reported in the newsletter FTC Watch.
Another option is that the FTC might require the divestiture of stores in cities where the two chains now compete, such as the Baltimore-Washington and Los Angeles areas.
Yet another possibility is that the latest deadline could be extended to permit further talks, a decision that would be made by the companies.

"We are continuing discussions with the FTC," said Todd Krasnow, executive vice president of marketing for Staples. "We don't comment on specific discussions. We anticipate in some fashion the deal will be transacted."

Together, Office Depot and Staples operate 1,117 superstores in the United States -- Staples 490 and Office Depot 527. The only other office superstore chain is OfficeMax. At issue in the talks has been the definition of the market served by the office superstores.
If office superstores compete primarily with each other, then the government might have qualms about permitting the number of competitors to shrink from three to two.
But representatives of Staples and Office Depot argue that they are a small part of a much larger market for office supplies and equipment.
They say their competitors include warehouse stores, office furniture stores, computer stores and even the corner pharmacy that sells school supplies.
The merger, first announced last September, has increasingly been the subject of public debate.

When the merger ran into delays this year, Office Depot and Staples took the unusual step of running full-page advertisements in newspapers around the country contending their combination would lead to lower prices for consumers.
Soon after the ads began running, consumer advocate Ralph Nader released a study that he said showed prices were lower in places where Office Depot and Staples competed directly against each other.
But in a commentary published in the Boston Globe this week, economist Lester Thurow argued that there was no reason to halt the merger.
"Market forces will keep Staples-Office Depot on a very tight leash," he said.
